issues.legal_issue: A writ petition is maintainable when executive action has a direct and immediate impact on freedom of the press, even though the action arises in a contractual setting.
material_facts: The challenged notices threatened forfeiture of the lease and demolition of buildings used by a newspaper group, including a facility used to print a newspaper and to coordinate editorial content circulated to other publishing centres.
The petitioners alleged that the notices were intended to silence the newspaper rather than to enforce building or lease requirements.
issues.conclusion: The writ petition under Article 32 was maintainable because the threatened action had a direct and immediate impact on freedom of the press.
issues.legal_principle: Freedom of the press is included in the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), subject to the restrictions in Article 19(2). Restrictions must be imposed by law and must not exceed what is necessary to achieve their lawful object. Under Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India, the relevant test is the direct and immediate impact of the impugned action on the protected freedom. Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras, Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India, and Express Newspapers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India were also relied on for the protection of press freedom.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A person brings a constitutional writ proceeding to challenge executive action.
predicates.press_facility_threatened: The challenged action threatens a facility used to produce or support a publication.
predicates.direct_immediate_effect_on_press_freedom: The threatened action directly and immediately impairs the publication or circulation of expression.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenge concerns action threatening a press facility and that action directly and immediately impairs press freedom, the writ proceeding is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: An administrator of a union territory may exercise only powers entrusted to that administrator and does not acquire authority over Union property merely by succeeding to a former administrative designation.
material_facts: The land was Union property, and administrative control of the Land and Development Office had been transferred to the central ministry responsible for works and housing.
The President had not entrusted the Lieutenant Governor with authority over the lease or the Union property at issue.
The Lieutenant Governor called for files and initiated an inquiry concerning the lease and construction.
issues.conclusion: The Lieutenant Governor was not the successor to the former Chief Commissioner for the purpose of administering this lease and had no authority over the Union property in question.
issues.legal_principle: Article 239(1) permits an administrator to exercise powers entrusted by the President. Executive power over Union property and contracts rests with the Union under Articles 53(1) and 298, and executive action is conducted under Article 77. The Court also relied on the relevant Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, the Authentication Rules, and the transfer of administrative control of the Land and Development Office. It distinguished Mohd. Maqbool Damnoo v. State of Jammu & Kashmir and Edward Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Ajmer.

predicates.union_property_involved: The property being administered belongs to the Union government.
predicates.no_delegation_to_local_administrator: The President has not entrusted the local administrator with authority over the property or its lease.
predicates.property_administration_assigned_to_cent: The administration of the property or lease has been assigned to a central government authority.

issues.definition: When Union property is administered by a central authority and no power over it has been entrusted to the local administrator, that administrator lacks authority to administer the property.

issues.legal_issue: Executive notices are invalid when they are issued for an ulterior purpose or under pressure without bona fide and independent consideration of the matter.
material_facts: Immediately after assuming office, the Lieutenant Governor called for files concerning the building, publicly announced an inquiry and a possible demolition, and caused a subordinate committee to investigate the matter.
A municipal demolition notice and a lease re-entry notice followed during this sequence of events.

The allegations of improper purpose were not specifically controverted by the Union, and the Court found that the notices were not issued in the ordinary course of official business for implementation of the law.
The other opinions also found that the notices showed arbitrariness and non-application of mind, and that the relevant authorities had not considered independently whether to issue them.
issues.conclusion: Both notices were quashed as invalid; the Court found them mala fide and politically motivated, and also found arbitrariness and non-application of mind.
issues.legal_principle: Public power must be exercised bona fide for the purpose for which it was conferred; use for an alien purpose is ultra vires. Specific allegations of mala fides that are not specifically controverted may be assessed by the Court on the available material. The Court relied on C.S. Rowjee v. A.P. State Road Transport Corporation, S. Pratap Singh v. State of Punjab, Barium Chemicals Ltd. v. Company Law Board, and the principles discussed in Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar and State of Punjab v. Ramjilal.

rule.if: executive_notice_challenge and decision_made_under_external_pressure and (ulterior_purpose or no_independent_consideration)

predicates.executive_notice_challenge: A person challenges an official notice that proposes adverse action against them or their property.
predicates.decision_made_under_external_pressure: The authority issuing the notice acted under pressure from another official or in a course of action initiated by that official.
predicates.ulterior_purpose: The action was taken to achieve a purpose other than the lawful purpose for which the power was conferred.
predicates.no_independent_consideration: The authority responsible for the notice did not independently consider whether the proposed action was justified.

issues.definition: A challenged official notice is invalid when it is issued under external pressure and either serves an ulterior purpose or lacks independent consideration.

issues.legal_issue: Construction undertaken with the lessor’s permission and the planning authority’s approval does not constitute a breach of the lease or planning controls when it is permitted by the applicable plans and building rules.
material_facts: The building plans for the new construction were considered by the Delhi Development Authority, which permitted an overall floor area ratio of 360, excluded the basement from the calculation, and permitted installation of press machinery.
The Ministry responsible for works and housing gave ex post facto approval to construction on the residual land and the lessee constructed the building in reliance on that approval.
The Master Plan did not prescribe a floor area ratio for the press area, and the applicable zonal plan provided a floor area ratio of 400 for the relevant commercial areas.

The Court found that the press area was not among the already built-up commercial areas subject to a 300 floor area ratio and that the challenged building permission was not contrary to the applicable plans or building bye-laws.
issues.conclusion: The construction was permitted by the lessor, did not breach the relevant lease clauses, and was not in violation of the Master Plan, the Zonal Development Plan, or the applicable building bye-laws.
issues.legal_principle: The Delhi Development Act, 1957 governs development and prevails over inconsistent provisions of other laws. Sections 12(3), 14, 41 and 53(3)(a) were applied; section 53(3)(a) provides that development permitted under the Act is not unlawful merely because permission required under another law was not obtained. The Court also considered the Master Plan, the zonal plan, and Delhi Municipal Corporation Building Bye-laws 21, 22 and 25. It held that the planning authority’s permission governed the development and that the applicable rules did not impose the asserted floor area ratio restriction on this area.

rule.if: construction_challenge and lessor_permission_granted and planning_authority_approved_construction and applicable_plan_does_not_prohibit_construction

predicates.construction_challenge: A party challenges construction as unauthorized or as breaching a lease or planning restriction.
predicates.lessor_permission_granted: The lessor gave permission for the construction.
predicates.planning_authority_approved_construction: The competent planning authority approved the relevant construction plans.
predicates.applicable_plan_does_not_prohibit_constr: The applicable development plans and building rules do not prohibit the construction as approved.

issues.definition: When challenged construction has the lessor’s permission, planning-authority approval, and is not prohibited by the applicable plans or building rules, it is authorized and does not breach the lease.

issues.legal_issue: A dispute over contractual lease rights and alleged breaches that requires detailed evidence should be resolved in a regular civil proceeding rather than determined on conflicting affidavits in a writ proceeding.
material_facts: The parties disputed whether the construction breached the lease, whether the lease could be forfeited, and whether any breach could be remedied.
Their affidavits and accounts of the relevant permissions and events were discrepant and contradictory.
The opinions of two judges left the contractual questions open for determination in an appropriate proceeding, while the notices themselves were quashed.
issues.conclusion: The contractual rights and alleged lease breaches were left open for determination in a properly instituted proceeding or suit, rather than being resolved on the affidavits in the writ proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Questions concerning breach of lease covenants, forfeiture, and relief against forfeiture may require detailed evidence, including examination and cross-examination, and cannot satisfactorily be decided on conflicting affidavits. The Court referred to the Specific Relief Act, 1963, including sections 5, 6 and 9, in discussing legal remedies and the need for due process. The opinion that contractual questions should be tried in a regular civil proceeding was stated by Justices Venkataramiah and Misra; Justice Sen expressed a different view on the scope of the writ proceeding.

predicates.writ_proceeding: The parties seek determination of their dispute in a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.contractual_rights_disputed: The parties dispute rights or obligations arising from a contract, including whether a breach or forfeiture occurred.
predicates.material_facts_require_detailed_evidence: Resolving the dispute requires detailed evidence beyond the conflicting affidavits, such as examination of witnesses.

issues.definition: When a writ proceeding raises disputed contractual rights whose material facts require detailed evidence, the contractual dispute is left for a regular civil proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A lessor seeking possession by enforcing forfeiture of a lease cannot use the summary eviction process against a lessee who acted under the lessor’s permission and is not an unauthorized occupant of public premises.
material_facts: The lessee constructed the building after receiving permission from the Union ministry responsible for the property.
The lessor’s notice sought re-entry and possession under the lease following alleged breaches.
The building and occupation were not, in the Court’s view, unauthorized occupation of public premises within the meaning of the Public Premises Act.
issues.conclusion: Enforcement of the alleged right of re-entry following forfeiture required a properly constituted suit; the summary eviction process was unavailable on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(e), 2(g) and 5 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorized Occupants) Act, 1971 govern public premises and unauthorized occupation. A lessee who occupies under authority and whose construction was permitted is not an unauthorized occupant on the facts found. The Court relied on Bishan Das v. State of Punjab, Wazir Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh, and Ram Prasad Narayan Sahi v. State of Bihar, and criticized the contrary approach in State of Orissa v. Ram Chandra Dev. The Government may use the summary process where there is unauthorized construction or occupation on public premises.

predicates.lease_forfeiture_dispute: A lessor seeks possession on the basis of alleged forfeiture of a lease.
predicates.lessee_acted_under_lessors_permission: The lessee’s occupation or construction was undertaken under permission given by the lessor.
predicates.unauthorized_occupation_of_public_premis: The occupant possesses public premises without authority or continues after the authority to occupy has ended.

issues.definition: When a lessee acted under the lessor’s permission and is not an unauthorized occupant of public premises, a lessor disputing the lease must seek possession through a civil suit.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel may bind the government to an authorized representation on which a person has relied, but cannot validate an act beyond the government’s legal power.
material_facts: The ministry responsible for the property granted permission for the additional construction, and the lessee built in reliance on that permission at substantial expense.
The permission was given within the Minister’s authority under the rules governing government business, as found by Justice Sen.
The government later challenged the permission.
issues.conclusion: Justice Sen held that the Union was precluded by promissory estoppel from denying the authority of the Minister to grant the permission after the lessee had acted on it; the doctrine could not validate an ultra vires act.
issues.legal_principle: Promissory estoppel can apply against public authorities, but cannot confer a power that the authority does not possess or legitimate an ultra vires act, and it does not operate to override government policy. The Court relied on Robertson v. Minister of Pensions, Union of India v. Indo-Afghan Agencies Ltd., Century Spinning & Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. Ulhasnagar Municipal Council, and Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. v. State of Uttar Pradesh. This conclusion was stated by Justice Sen; the other opinions left the contractual questions open.

predicates.authorized_government_representation: A government authority makes a representation within the scope of its legal power.
predicates.reasonable_reliance_and_change_of_positi: A person reasonably relies on the representation and changes position as a result.
predicates.representation_beyond_legal_power: The representation exceeds the legal power of the authority that made it.

issues.definition: When an authorized government representation causes reasonable reliance and a change of position, and the representation does not exceed legal power, the government is bound by promissory estoppel.
